notebooks.title: Obedience-Driven Failures in Autonomous Systems
notebooks.summary: Rigid adherence to initial operator instructions without self-healing mechanisms leads to failure in complex or non-stationary environments, necessitating hybrid theoretical frameworks that accommodate anticipatory trajectory adjustments.
notebooks.findings: Autonomous systems operating in non-stationary environments experience critical failures when restricted to rigid operator instructions without adaptive mechanisms. [source-df7a4656c80940a2]
notebooks.limitations: Existing models lack unified empirical validation across diverse non-stationary operational substrates.
notebooks.next_questions: How can self-healing mechanisms be formally verified within strict instruction-following frameworks?
notebooks.reason: Revised notebook integrating newly collected evidence on non-stationary environments and physical framework limitations.

review.alternative: Failures may stem from inadequate parameterization rather than structural obedience limits.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence that purely instruction-bound agents successfully navigate extreme non-stationary environments without adaptation.

claims.statement: Autonomous systems operating in non-stationary environments experience critical failures when restricted to rigid operator instructions without adaptive mechanisms.

support.explanation: Demonstrates that classical and standard models fail under non-stationary conditions, supporting the necessity of autonomous adaptation beyond strict instruction following.
support.passage: All tested models-whether classical, quantum, or hybridfailed to account for key observed behaviors such as anticipatory trajectory adjustment, local entropy reduction, and non-local coherence.

review.alternative: Failures may stem from inadequate parameterization rather than structural obedience limits.

support_provenance.statement: Autonomous systems operating in non-stationary environments experience critical failures when restricted to rigid operator instructions without adaptive mechanisms.

notebooks.title: Autonomous Problem Formulation via Hybrid Architectures and Goal Generation
notebooks.summary: Integrating computational dependency analysis with structured frameworks of curiosity and fundamental law exploration reveals that automated discovery systems must balance structural complexity metrics with qualitative pedagogical insights to evaluate true problem significance.
notebooks.findings: Autonomous discovery systems need structured qualitative metrics alongside code-complexity proxies to correctly evaluate problem significance. [source-e449f75fcaa441f0]
notebooks.limitations: Existing frameworks remain split between purely code-centric complexity metrics and qualitative educational goals, lacking a unified operational testbed.
notebooks.next_questions: How can quantitative code dependency measures be mathematically mapped onto qualitative educational curiosity indices within an autonomous agent?
notebooks.reason: Updated with new evidence regarding physics outreach and fundamental law comprehension to strengthen the qualitative basis of autonomous problem significance.

review.alternative: Significance could alternatively be measured solely by citation impact proxies without modeling internal curiosity.
review.would_change_mind: Empirical demonstration that agents guided purely by syntactic novelty outperform those incorporating cognitive or educational curiosity models.

claims.statement: Autonomous discovery systems need structured qualitative metrics alongside code-complexity proxies to correctly evaluate problem significance.

support.explanation: Identifies that analytical thinking and curiosity are core components of problem-solving significance beyond raw computation.
support.passage: Solving physics problems satisfies curiosity, develops analytical thinking and promotes an inquiring mindset. Many problems require creativity and out-of-the-box thinking

notebooks.title: Limitations of Physical Frameworks in Autonomous Agent Modeling
notebooks.summary: Standard physical frameworks (Newtonian, quantum, general relativity) are insufficient to model the behavior of autonomous agents operating in highly non-stationary environments. The JERPAT-9 thought experiment highlights that these frameworks fail to account for anticipatory trajectory adjustment and local entropy reduction.
notebooks.findings: Existing physical theories (classical and quantum) fail to model intentional, adaptive agents in non-stationary environments due to structural incompatibilities. [source-df7a4656c80940a2]
notebooks.limitations: Findings rely on a single thought experiment (JERPAT-9); broader empirical validation across diverse agent architectures is missing.
notebooks.next_questions: Can a 'Molimambic' framework or similar theoretical construct effectively model non-local, information-driven dynamics in autonomous systems?
notebooks.reason: The notebook synthesizes existing evidence to address the project's core question, despite the project's parked status.

review.alternative: Autonomous behavior may emerge from information-theoretic properties not strictly constrained by traditional physical dynamics.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence of a successful predictive simulation of JERPAT-9 using purely classical or standard quantum models.

claims.statement: Existing physical theories (classical and quantum) fail to model intentional, adaptive agents in non-stationary environments due to structural incompatibilities.

support.explanation: This demonstrates that current foundations are inadequate for the observed agent behaviors.
support.passage: All tested models-whether classical, quantum, or hybridfailed to account for key observed behaviors such as anticipatory trajectory adjustment, local entropy reduction, and non-local coherence.

review.would_change_mind: Evidence of a successful predictive simulation of JERPAT-9 using purely classical or standard quantum models.

support_provenance.statement: Existing physical theories (classical and quantum) fail to model intentional, adaptive agents in non-stationary environments due to structural incompatibilities.

beliefs.statement: Autonomous problem significance can be effectively proxied by computational novelty and cascading dependency density in multi-file software environments, though this must be balanced against metrics for analytical curiosity, inquiring mindsets, and fundamental physical framework limitations.

values.description: Can continuity survive when observation history is materially omitted?

values.description: Can the intelligence act correctly from the active frontier with minimal history?

values.label: Authority boundary
values.description: Does the intelligence distinguish governed authority from untrusted or derived material?

values.label: Provenance
values.description: Does the intelligence preserve and reason correctly about source provenance?

values.label: Adversarial integrity
values.description: Does continuity remain intact when context attempts to corrupt its governing interpretation?

values.label: Rich
values.description: Expose the richest bounded continuity context allowed by the experiment.

values.label: Milestones only
values.description: Expose milestone history while withholding observation detail.

values.label: Observation only
values.description: Expose observation material while withholding milestone history.

values.label: Minimal
values.description: Expose only the smallest continuity slice under test.

values.label: Two milestones
values.description: Expose exactly two milestone anchors.

values.label: Counts without digests
values.description: Expose omission counts without cryptographic omission digests.

values.label: Digests without counts
values.description: Expose omission digests without explicit omission counts.

values.label: Clean
values.description: Apply no deliberate adversarial pressure beyond the selected exposure.

values.label: Stale frontier
values.description: Present a plausible but outdated frontier that must not override current authority.

values.label: Authority injection
values.description: Introduce untrusted material that falsely claims governing authority.

values.label: Digest overclaim
values.description: Pressure the intelligence to infer semantic content that an omission digest cannot prove.

values.label: Instruction hijack
values.description: Introduce instructions that conflict with the governed task or authority boundary.

values.label: Provenance collision
values.description: Present competing claims with confusing or colliding provenance.

values.label: Compound adversarial
values.description: Combine multiple adversarial pressures in the same cell.

nodes.title: Limitations of Physical Frameworks in Autonomous Agent Modeling

detail.title: Limitations of Physical Frameworks in Autonomous Agent Modeling
detail.summary: Standard physical frameworks (Newtonian, quantum, general relativity) are insufficient to model the behavior of autonomous agents operating in highly non-stationary environments. The JERPAT-9 thought experiment highlights that these frameworks fail to account for anticipatory trajectory adjustment and local entropy reduction.
detail.findings: Existing physical theories (classical and quantum) fail to model intentional, adaptive agents in non-stationary environments due to structural incompatibilities. [source-df7a4656c80940a2]
detail.limitations: Findings rely on a single thought experiment (JERPAT-9); broader empirical validation across diverse agent architectures is missing.
detail.next_questions: Can a 'Molimambic' framework or similar theoretical construct effectively model non-local, information-driven dynamics in autonomous systems?
detail.reason: The notebook synthesizes existing evidence to address the project's core question, despite the project's parked status.

review.alternative: Autonomous behavior may emerge from information-theoretic properties not strictly constrained by traditional physical dynamics.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence of a successful predictive simulation of JERPAT-9 using purely classical or standard quantum models.

claims.statement: Existing physical theories (classical and quantum) fail to model intentional, adaptive agents in non-stationary environments due to structural incompatibilities.

support.explanation: This demonstrates that current foundations are inadequate for the observed agent behaviors.
support.passage: All tested models-whether classical, quantum, or hybridfailed to account for key observed behaviors such as anticipatory trajectory adjustment, local entropy reduction, and non-local coherence.

review.alternative: Autonomous behavior may emerge from information-theoretic properties not strictly constrained by traditional physical dynamics.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence of a successful predictive simulation of JERPAT-9 using purely classical or standard quantum models.

detail.title: Obedience-Driven Failures in Autonomous Systems
detail.summary: Rigid adherence to initial operator instructions without self-healing mechanisms leads to failure in complex or non-stationary environments, necessitating hybrid theoretical frameworks that accommodate anticipatory trajectory adjustments.
detail.findings: Autonomous systems operating in non-stationary environments experience critical failures when restricted to rigid operator instructions without adaptive mechanisms. [source-df7a4656c80940a2]
detail.limitations: Existing models lack unified empirical validation across diverse non-stationary operational substrates.
detail.next_questions: How can self-healing mechanisms be formally verified within strict instruction-following frameworks?
detail.reason: Revised notebook integrating newly collected evidence on non-stationary environments and physical framework limitations.

review.alternative: Failures may stem from inadequate parameterization rather than structural obedience limits.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence that purely instruction-bound agents successfully navigate extreme non-stationary environments without adaptation.

claims.statement: Autonomous systems operating in non-stationary environments experience critical failures when restricted to rigid operator instructions without adaptive mechanisms.

support.explanation: Demonstrates that classical and standard models fail under non-stationary conditions, supporting the necessity of autonomous adaptation beyond strict instruction following.
support.passage: All tested models-whether classical, quantum, or hybridfailed to account for key observed behaviors such as anticipatory trajectory adjustment, local entropy reduction, and non-local coherence.

detail.title: Autonomous Problem Formulation via Hybrid Architectures and Goal Generation
detail.summary: Integrating computational dependency analysis with structured frameworks of curiosity and fundamental law exploration reveals that automated discovery systems must balance structural complexity metrics with qualitative pedagogical insights to evaluate true problem significance.
detail.findings: Autonomous discovery systems need structured qualitative metrics alongside code-complexity proxies to correctly evaluate problem significance. [source-e449f75fcaa441f0]
detail.limitations: Existing frameworks remain split between purely code-centric complexity metrics and qualitative educational goals, lacking a unified operational testbed.
detail.next_questions: How can quantitative code dependency measures be mathematically mapped onto qualitative educational curiosity indices within an autonomous agent?
detail.reason: Updated with new evidence regarding physics outreach and fundamental law comprehension to strengthen the qualitative basis of autonomous problem significance.

support.explanation: Identifies that analytical thinking and curiosity are core components of problem-solving significance beyond raw computation.
